summary.text: Take \(p=29\), for which \(29\equiv9\pmod{20}\) and \(29=3^2+5\cdot2^2\). Since the formal statement does not tie the universally quantified \(x,y\) to this representation, it forces the same sum to be congruent to both \(-58\) (using \(x=0\)) and \(-54\) (using \(x=1\)) modulo \(29^2=841\), an impossibility.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-4)^k\binom nk^2\binom{n-k}{k}^2.
\]
This is the same sequence as in the displayed binomial-sum description, since
\[
\binom nk\binom{n-k}{k}=\binom n{2k}\binom{2k}{k},
\]
and both sides vanish in the relevant sense when \(2k>n\). For a prime \(p\), put
\[
S_p=\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}a(n).
\]
Also write
\[
R_5(N)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{there exist integers }u,v\text{ such that }N=u^2+5v^2.
\]

The accepted formal version of the conjecture has an important quantifier structure. In its first case it asserts that, whenever \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {20}\), then for every pair of integers \(x,y\),
\[
R_5(p)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
S_p\equiv 4x^2-2p\pmod {p^2}.
\]
Notice that the variables witnessing \(R_5(p)\) are existentially quantified inside the definition of \(R_5\), and are not the displayed variables \(x,y\) occurring on the right-hand side. Thus, as soon as \(p\) has any representation by the quadratic form, the asserted congruence must hold for every independently selected integer \(x\) (and every \(y\)). We show that this assertion is inconsistent.

Take
\[
p=29.
\]
This is prime: any proper prime divisor would be at most \(\sqrt{29}<6\), but \(29\) is divisible by none of \(2,3,5\). It is also distinct from \(2\) and \(5\), as required by the statement. Moreover,
\[
29\equiv9\pmod {20},
\]
so the first branch of the asserted congruence applies. Finally,
\[
29=3^2+5\cdot2^2=9+20,
\]
so \(R_5(29)\) is true.

Now apply the universal assertion first with the independently chosen values \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). The hypothesis \(R_5(29)\) remains true because it is witnessed by \((u,v)=(3,2)\), not by the selected pair \((x,y)\). We consequently obtain
\[
S_{29}\equiv4\cdot0^2-2\cdot29=-58\pmod {29^2}.
\]

Apply the same assertion a second time with \(x=1\) and \(y=0\). Again the representation hypothesis is the already established existential fact \(29=3^2+5\cdot2^2\). This gives
\[
S_{29}\equiv4\cdot1^2-2\cdot29=-54\pmod {29^2}.
\]

Two integers congruent to the same integer modulo a modulus must be congruent to each other modulo that modulus. Explicitly, the first congruence says that \(29^2\mid S_{29}+58\), while the second says that \(29^2\mid S_{29}+54\). Subtracting these divisibilities would imply
\[
29^2\mid (S_{29}+58)-(S_{29}+54)=4.
\]
But \(29^2=841\), and \(841\nmid4\). Equivalently,
\[
-58\not\equiv-54\pmod {841},
\]
because their difference is \(4\), which is nonzero and has absolute value less than \(841\).

This contradiction disproves the universally quantified proposition. No evaluation of \(S_{29}\), and hence no evaluation of the individual binomial sums, is needed: whatever integer \(S_{29}\) is, it cannot simultaneously lie in the two distinct residue classes \(-58\) and \(-54\) modulo \(841\).

The source of the counterexample should be made explicit. It disproves the accepted formal proposition because that proposition separates the existential witnesses in \(R_5(p)\) from the variables \(x,y\) appearing in \(4x^2-2p\). It does not by itself refute the differently quantified intended statement in which the hypothesis is literally \(p=x^2+5y^2\) for the same \(x,y\) used in the conclusion. For that intended statement, choosing \(x=0\) or \(x=1\) at \(p=29\) would not satisfy the representation equation. The disproof above is nevertheless a complete counterexample to the accepted conjecture statement: at the admissible prime \(29\), its first clause forces two incompatible congruences.
